newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Thai Buddhas beam benignly in Belgium.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Thai Buddhas beam benignly in Belgium.

text.p: They travel very rarely. Indeed, most have never left home before.
But the journey half way round the globe has seemingly had no adverse effects on the more than 100 Thai Buddhas on show for the first time in Belgium.

There are Buddhas small and large as well as the gilded head of one giant statue from the old Siamese capital of Ayutthaya. They are made from stone, gold, bronze, silver and wood, and their ages range from 2000 years B.C to the 19th century A.D.
Most are in the bhumisparsa-mudra position, sitting cross-legged with the left hand lying palm up in the lap and the right hand palm down on the right knee.
This classic position, with the right hand pointing down towards the goddess of earth, symbolises the achievement of enlightenment and the defeat of evil.
Some of the other depictions of the Buddha symbolise the descent from heaven and the absence of fear.
But regardless of their age or the symbolism of the different positions of the hands, the one feature all the Buddhas have in common is the inscrutably serene expression on their faces.

"I am sure that, through viewing of these art treasures, the Belgian public will be able to enhance their understanding of the history, culture and social fabric that have made Thailand a vibrant and happy society," Somkiati Ariyapruchya, Bangkok's ambassador to Belgium, said in a foreward to a guide book to the exhibition, which will remain in Brussels until February 16.

The tastefully-mounted exhibition, set in the tranquility of Brussels' Parc du Cinquantenaire nestling next to the headquarters of the often not so tranquil European Union, projects an aura of calm, although lacking the gentle aroma of burning joss-sticks that pervades Thai temples.
It is a timely message to a Belgium caught up in a national scandal of child murder, political assassination and suspicion of police and judicial bungling or worse.
The fact that the display is in Belgium at all is a tribute to the close personal relationship between Thailand's King Bhumibol Adulyadej and King Baudouin of Belgium, who died in August 1993.

The exhibition is in part to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the coronation of the 68-year-old Thai king who is revered in his country as a demi-god, and partly to reaffirm the personal links the U.S.-born Bhumibol has to the Belgian royal family.
Most of the 120 Buddhas and artefacts on show come from Bangkok museum, although one is from the king's personal collection.

While the basic image of the Buddha has remained unchanged for centuries, cultural and social developments have left their mark as each successive generation has tried to give the deity a flavour of the time.

"There are certain rules of iconography but, at the same time, for the expression it depends on the period and the artist," Prince Subhadradis Diskul, a professor at Bangkok's Silpakorn University, told Reuters.
"You might say that in the Utong period it was rather severe but in the Sukothai art he is always smiling gently," he added.

Regardless of the individual expression or posture of each Buddha, each is believed by the Thais to embody a spark of the essential spirit of the original Buddha or enlightened one, Siddhartha Gautama.
Theravada Buddhism is the dominant religion in Thailand -- known until 1939 as Siam -- where 90 percent of the 60 million population is Buddhist.

This form of Buddhism differs from other forms by not recognising the pantheon of bodhisattvas, or enlightened beings, who have chosen to delay their entry to Nirvana in order to encourage humans to follow their lead.
